Syllables with voiced plosives, affricates or fricatives are in low register tone (g, j, dr, d, b, dz, zh, z, zhr). Syllables with voiceless or aspirated initials, including voiceless liquids and fricatives, are in the high register tone (k, kh, c, ch, tr, thr, t, th, p, ph, ts, tsh, sh, s, h, hy, lh, shr, hr). Only Bumthang syllables beginning with a voiced continuant (ng, ny, n, m, y, r, l, w, or a vowel) may be in either the preglottalised high or the low register tone.' van Driem's grammar (the fullest description, 77 pp.) has no stress or accent statement at all (only 'accent' hits are the circumflex diacritic). Peck 2017 sec. 1.1.1: at least nine tonal contrasts on monosyllables (Donohue p.c.); the prosodic word is defined by a single tonal contour. Stress in the sense of the registers: the one 2020 sentence, hedged by its author.

2069.tone: Binary H/L tone; syllables H, L, <HL>, <LH>, rarely <LHL>; stem/word melodies {H}, {L}, {HL}, {LH}, {LHL}. Nouns carry lexical melodies /HL/, /LH/, /L/ (virtually no minimal pairs; bóyè 'watermelon' vs bòyè 'mosquito', sé 'horse' vs sè 'foot'); verbs have grammatical, not lexical, tone; tonosyntactic overlays {LH} (noun before adjective) and {HL} (possessed noun); Rightward H-Spreading HL#L > HH#L. On stress/accent the grammar says: 'absence of an elaborated stress/accent system' (p.27); one-H-per-word tendency gives 'a resemblance to pitch-accent systems' (p.5); phonetic pitch-and-intensity peak on the last H before the tone break (p.29); an accentual reanalysis is floated on p.29 and p.59 ('if we reanalyse /HL/ melody in terms of a stem-initial tonal accent') but the grammar keeps a tonal description; all-H strings before numeral '2' 'go against the pitch-accent tendencies of the rest of the language' (p.86). No dedicated stress section; the word 'stress' occurs once in the whole grammar (p.27).

2070.heavy: Any syllable whose vowel is not marked with the breve ('signe de brièveté'). p. 6 lists three vowel quantities in columns, 'a moyen. ā long ă bref.', so unmarked (medium) and macron-marked (long) vowels bear the stress and breve-marked short vowels are skipped. The criterion is vowel quantity (short vs non-short); coded CVV to match the published catalog's alii1240 entry (Calloc'h's parallel 1911 Gbéa sketch, same criterion, adjudicated weight-sensitive, stated with hedges / CVV) and the sister ngba1284 record of this run (same page, same sentence, CVV). Note the heavy class is 'non-short' (medium or long), not 'long only'.

2070.prule: Intensity stress ('accent tonique', a 'coup de voix' without appreciable pitch rise) ordinarily falls on the first syllable of the word that is not marked with the sign of shortness (breve = short vowel, p. 6 'ă bref'), i.e. the leftmost syllable whose vowel is not short. A separate pitch accent ('accent de hauteur', acute) sits on a monosyllable or on one or more syllables of the same word.

2070.tone: Calloc'h separates an 'accent de hauteur' (pitch rise, marked by the acute, on a monosyllable or on one or more syllables of the same word) from the intensity stress; p. 6 lists the acute as 'accent de hauteur' and the tilde as the nasality sign. Modern work in the copy consulted describes Gbanzili as a three-register (H/M/L) tone language and says nothing about stress: Rombi 1994 ('Considérations phonético-phonologiques': tone registers in loan adaptation) and Boyeldieu 2013 (grammatical marking 'par leur identité tonale', citing Rombi & Thomas 2006); neither text contains 'accent' or 'stress' in the relevant sense. tn.quote: Alle Textbeispiele sind tonal bezeichnet. Dabei werden Hochton mit (´), Steigton mit (ˇ) und Fallton mit (^) markiert, Tiefton bleibt unbezeichnet. Eine systematische Tonologie kann noch nicht gegeben werden, jedoch ist deutlich, daß tonale Unterschiede kaum eine lexikalische, aber eine stärkere grammatische Bedeutung haben. Dies wird bei der Darstellung der nominalen und der verbalen Flexion deutlich werden. ... Es können zwei tonal markierte Kasus unterschieden werden ... Auch variieren die Töne dialektal ... tn.translation: All text examples are marked for tone. High tone is marked with (´), rising tone with (ˇ) and falling tone with (^); low tone is left unmarked. A systematic tonology cannot yet be given, but it is clear that tonal differences have hardly any lexical significance but a stronger grammatical one. This will become clear in the presentation of nominal and verbal inflection. ... Two tonally marked cases can be distinguished ... The tones also vary by dialect ... Without a tonological analysis no more precise statements can be made.

tn.translation: 4. TONES Tone (that is, the musical level of each syllable pronounced) plays a very important role in the spoken language. The Bwisi language has two basic tones: the high tone and the low tone. There are pairs of words distinguished by their tones. E.g.: itutu 'measles' - itútu 'flask'; ubaghana 'to be fooled' - ubághana 'to quarrel'. Tone is also important for indicating tense in verb conjugation. But in most cases the context makes the meaning clear, and there is no need to mark tones in writing.

Howard 1967 p. 80: 'Every word contains one phonemic strong stress which may occur on either the penultimate or the final syllable ... Since it most often occurs on the penultimate syllable, it is written only when it occurs on the final syllable.'

2084.heavy: No weight rule. Closed final syllables take penult stress (bastok, benach), i.e. codas do not attract stress; the only phonological attractor the author entertains is final -an ('it could instead be that there is something (phonological) about final -an that attracts stress'). Final stress needs nucleus /a o e/; /i u ɨ/ never stressed in the ultima.
2084.prule: Stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive) within a right-edge two-syllable window: one stress per word, on the penult by default and on the ultima in a lexically or morphologically marked minority (nouns in open -a/-o, words in -an incl. all verb infinitives, the clitic té 'day'); never earlier than the penult; minimal pair ena 'pure' vs ená 'seller'. Howard 1967: every word has one phonemic strong stress, penultimate or final, penult most frequent.
2084.srule: None: 'Every word contains one phonemic strong stress which may occur on either the penultimate or the final syllable' (Howard 1967 sec. 4.1 p. 80); not mentioned in O'Brien 2018 sec. 2.4 'Stress' pp. 46-47. 2086.prule: A strong dynamic (stress) accent is reconstructed: only the accented vowel of a word is preserved/written, all other vowels are deleted or unwritten (a post-tonic [i] may survive). 2089.dq: Sidwell 2018 p.105: "the rightmost syllable of lexical roots bears the primary word stress". Braine 1970 p.69: "The rules are presented here according to which portion of the word they apply to: pretonic, tonic, and post-tonic, or inter-tonic syllables." (Braine's stress allophony and the default-placement rule are stated over the macrosegment, i.e. the intonational phrase: p.34 "the unit within …
2089.prule: Primary stress is an inherent property of (root) morphemes: it falls on the final syllable of the lexical root (roots are one- or two-syllable iambs, CVC / CVCVC, e.g. kuléh, taníy, kumyéh); prefixes and infixes are unstressed and suffixes are mostly unstressed, so the surface position in the word depends on the morphology (word-final in bare roots, penult/antepenult when suffixes follow). Braine states the position is predictable 'almost entirely' from the grammatical class of morphemes; if no morpheme in the macrosegment is inherently stressed, default primary stress goes to the first syllable of the macrosegment.
2089.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress is described. Braine's 'secondary' [ˋ] and 'tertiary' [ˇ] stresses are positional allophones of the one strong-stress phoneme /ˊ/, graded within the macrosegment (phrase): a strong stress between two others is tertiary, the last one in the macrosegment is full primary (absent emphatic stress), others are secondary (sec.151, pp.34-35). Within a word a second strong stress is morphological: a CVC suffix syllable following the stressed root usually also bears /ˊ/ (pp.173-174; sí·phə́trɛ, cɨ́khukú·ʔ), its strength relative to the root stress being set by phrase position. Braine notes prosody was little investigated (p.39).
2089.quote: Braine 1970 p.34: "There are three contrastive degrees of stress: primary, weak, and emphatic." pp.39-40: "Little time was spent with the informant working out prosodic problems; this was an unfortunate omission as many questions have been left unanswered by the available data. ... Given knowledge of the grammatical class of morphemes it is possible to predict almost entirely which syllables will have primary stress; pitch level prediction and function however have not thus far yielded to analysis." p.71: "//-n- kuléh// → //kunléh// 'what is thrown' //-m- taníy// → //tamníy// 'five only' ... …

evidence_works.work: von Sowa 1887, Die Mundart der slovakischen Zigeuner (Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, X+194 pp.; Lautlehre IV. Accent, § 21, pp. 41-46)
evidence_works.detail: Describes the Slovak Romani of Trencsén-Teplicz (West Slovakia) as recorded 1884-85, not the Eastern Uzh variety the entry is keyed to. Reports the inherited paroxytone (penultimate) principle in open conflict with Slovak initial stress and 'nahezu aufgegeben' (p. 11): no oxytones, all disyllables initial; trisyllables with short penult mostly initial-stressed (kókalos, číriklo, ákanak) with many penultimate exceptions (manúša, kapál'i, loans in -aris); trisyllables with long closed penult mostly penultimate (labárdi, manúšni, dadéske); words of more than three syllables with short penult carry main stress on the initial syllable and a secondary stress (Nebenton) on the penult, the reverse with a long penult (p. 45); genitives in -kero antepenultimate (čāvéskero, p. 45); the negation na/ma always takes main stress before the verb (ná darau, p. 45); monosyllabic nouns throw stress back onto the article before a stressed syllable (ó rom gēlas, p. 46), which parallels Beníšek's é daj, ó phral.

2091.heavy: Not stated in weight terms. The only structural remark: word pairs contrasting in accent all have a single consonant between penult and ultima; words with a medial consonant cluster show no accent contrast (CVCCV with final glottal stop: invariably penult; CVCCVC: ultima ~ penult in free variation within one speaker).
2091.prule: Accent is phonemic (lexically contrastive) within a right-edge window: the final syllable is the usual and unmarked position, the penult (realised as vowel length) is a frequent alternative, and a small number of words have antepenultimate accent; minimal pairs differ by accent alone (anak 'child' / 'anak 'children', sulat 'lime container' / 'sulat 'letter'). No syllable-count or weight rule predicts the position.
2091.srule: Not mentioned in Headland & Healey 1974 (sec. 2.1 'Accent' pp. 4-5; secs. 2-3 pp. 4-7ff. read; PL C-28 reprint pp. vii, xii-xiii): the accent section describes one accent per word (intonation peak; loudness when final, length when penult) and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.
